extracted.intended_audience: students, critics, and practitioners of drama/playwrights studying Aristotelian dramatic theory
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for composing and evaluating tragic drama according to Aristotelian principles (unity, plot structure, and tragic character). Focuses on how action should be organized, temporal/spatial constraints, the role of chorus, and the qualities of the ideal tragic hero.

rubrics_metrics.name: Unity of Action
rubrics_metrics.description: The only dramatic Unity enjoined by Aristotle is Unity of Action: the action must be an organic structure directed to a single end.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Unity is the higher and controlling law of the drama. All parts (thoughts, emotions, decisions, external events) must be inextricably interwoven and converge on a definite point; minor effects must be subordinated to an ever-growing unity. The supreme test of unity is the powerful, concentrated impression in which the end reveals the meaning of the whole. Avoid subordinating Unity of Action to rules about time/place.

rubrics_metrics.name: Causal sequence (cause and effect)
rubrics_metrics.description: Within the dramatic action a strict sequence of cause and effect is prescribed; 'follows' marks a causal, not purely temporal, sequence.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Place events so that each follows as a necessary or probable consequence of what precedes; the causal chain should not be indefinitely extended outwards. The middle must be causally connected to both beginning and end. Use causal necessity/probability (εἰκός / ἀναγκαῖον) to justify events; avoid loose succession of scenes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definitions of beginning, middle, and end
rubrics_metrics.description: Beginning: that which does not require something to precede it (relative beginning). Middle: that which follows something and is followed by something (causally connected). End: must conclude the action.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ensure the beginning, middle, and end are not arbitrarily chosen; the beginning should not depend on prior events, the middle must link to before and after, and the end must properly conclude the action. Exclude plots with beginnings requiring external precedent, endings that leave action unconcluded, or middles standing alone.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid episodic (epeisodic) plotting
rubrics_metrics.description: A succession of stirring scenes does not make a tragedy; episodic plots are condemned where scenes follow one another without inward connexion (εἰκός or ἀναγκαῖον).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not rely on a sequence of striking situations, rapid contrasts, surprises, or 'pathetic effects' disconnected by lack of causal link (the text criticizes Euripides for this). Each scene should contribute causally and thematically to the central action.

rubrics_metrics.name: Organic synthesis (σύστασις / σύνθεσις)
rubrics_metrics.description: The union of parts should be vital and organic, not a mechanical piecing together of incidents.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Compose the plot so parts constitute a living whole; the recurring Poetics phrase σύστασις indicates vital union. Analytical isolation of elements is for study, but composition must aim for organic integration revealed by causal connection and a single purpose.

rubrics_metrics.name: Convergence to a single end
rubrics_metrics.description: The whole series of events and moral forces are directed to a single end; the action converges on a definite point and the thread of purpose becomes more marked as it advances.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Arrange events so they accumulate impulse toward an inevitable catastrophe or resolution; the end should illuminate the meaning of the whole. Use Lowell's notion that each scene should lead by a logic to something that follows, contributing toward the inevitable catastrophe.

rubrics_metrics.name: Concentration and compression of dramatic action
rubrics_metrics.description: Drama should be more compact and serried than epic: incidents should be never mere incidents and sequence of parts should be more inevitable and morally more necessary.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Favor concentrated action that presses toward a controlling end; avoid including many independent minor actions (πολύμυθος) typical of epic. Keep incidental material tightly integrated or omit it.

rubrics_metrics.name: Role of episodes and retarding incidents (epic contrast)
rubrics_metrics.description: Epic may admit many episodes and 'retarding' incidents that delay the dénouement; drama generally should not.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recognize genre difference: epic can pause, diversify and describe simultaneous/collateral incidents; drama, presented in the present, should avoid lengthy diversions that do not serve the central conflict.

rubrics_metrics.name: Chorus as unifying and temporal device
rubrics_metrics.description: The Chorus forms an ideal bond between separate parts of action and can 'release us from the captivity of time' — choral odes suspend outward action and idealize time.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use choral/lyrical interludes (or analogous devices) to bridge scenes, modulate perceived time, and maintain unity. The choral interval's duration is poetically determined and can cover events imaginatively without literal representation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Unity of Time (practice, not strict rule)
rubrics_metrics.description: Tragedy 'endeavours, as far as possible, to confine itself to a single revolution of the sun' (the dramatic action is generally limited to about a day), but this is a rough generalisation, not a strict law.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prefer to keep dramatic action within a limited time-scope to preserve intensity, but recognize historical exceptions (Eumenides, Trachiniae, Supplices, Agamemnon). Do not rigidly force an implausible compression solely to obey a clock-rule.

rubrics_metrics.name: Unity of Place (stage-practice/derivative)
rubrics_metrics.description: Unity of Place was commonly observed in Greek tragedy as stage-practice but is not directly enjoined by the Poetics; critics later deduced it from Unity of Time.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use a single or narrowly conceived locale when it serves unity, but do not let artificial constraints on place impede the inner logic of character and events. Historical insistence on place (e.g., French rules) sometimes produced awkward contrivances.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of verisimilitude/probability when strict realism fails
rubrics_metrics.description: When strict equivalence of action-time to representation-time cannot be achieved, Aristotle supplies the defect of necessity by probability (εἰκός)—verisimilitude that will 'cheat' the audience into acceptance.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Rely on probability/credibility to bridge gaps in realistic detail; avoid puerile devices that attempt to equate representation exactly with reality. The audience will accept reasonable poetic license if the internal logic and probability are maintained.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid subordinating Unity of Action to Time/Place rules
rubrics_metrics.description: Do not let the minor unities (time/place) override the higher Unity of Action; excessive adherence to time/place can compress action and violate inner consistency of character.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prioritize the integrity of character development and causal necessity over rigid clock- or location-based constraints. Historical French practice compressed incidents into limited hours and sometimes forced characters into unnatural movements—avoid such compromises.

rubrics_metrics.name: Dramatic idealization of place and time (poetic transport)
rubrics_metrics.description: The drama requires a certain idealisation of place and time; the poet transports the audience to a distant land/age, and the imagination ignores strict calendrical reckoning.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use imaginative invocation of setting and time to focus attention on the action; do not concern the audience with exact hours or dates unless required by the drama. Shakespearean freedom with place/time is cited positively.

rubrics_metrics.name: Tragic hero: evoke katharsis of pity and fear
rubrics_metrics.description: The function of tragedy is to produce the katharsis of pity and fear; characters and catastrophe must be such as to arouse these emotions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Design plot and character so that pity is felt for undeserved suffering and fear for similarity to ourselves. The plot must enable a full satisfaction of these emotions through reversal and recognition as appropriate.

rubrics_metrics.name: Qualities of the ideal tragic hero
rubrics_metrics.description: The tragic hero should be neither eminently good nor utterly bad; he 'leans to the side of goodness' and falls through some great flaw or 'fatal error' (ἁμαρτία), not through deliberate vice.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Portray a character of high rank/fortune whose misfortune arises from error or moral failing rather than pure wickedness; this elicits both pity and fear and renders the catastrophe striking. Avoid making the protagonist wholly virtuous (which shocks) or wholly villainous (which arouses only moral satisfaction).

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid happy endings and double-thread plots
rubrics_metrics.description: Plots that give prosperity to the good and misfortune to the bad (double catastrophe or 'happy ending') produce τὸ φιλάνθρωπον (satisfaction to moral sense) rather than proper tragic effect.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Resist constructing dual-thread narratives or 'happy' resolutions aimed merely to gratify the audience; such structures commonly pass as pleasing but fail to achieve the tragic katharsis. The unity and single trajectory of tragic action are compromised by double plots.
